Introduce yourself. Today we review FedHome, a 2026 paper from Computer Networks. We explain what it proposes, what it achieved, then critically examine the evidence and propose corrections.

Explain the choice: it is recent, it is about something everyone uses at home, it combines the three main topics of our course, and it is about privacy-preserving AI, a fast-growing area. Most importantly for a critique, it uses public datasets and reports detailed tables, so we could check the numbers ourselves. We picked it from six candidate papers our teacher allowed.

BSP means Broadband Service Provider, an ISP. Homes are full of IoT devices. When the network slows, the customer blames the ISP, but the ISP cannot look inside the home without violating privacy. The pills are the four requirements the paper sets.

Part 2 · The method

How FedHome works

Learning happens inside every home. Only small model updates travel to the provider, never the raw traffic.

Transition: now that we know the problem, here is the solution the authors propose and how they tested it.

The proposal

FedHome trains inside each home and shares only the model

1

Gateway

Profile the home

An initial gateway model identifies devices once, with ARP-spoofing scans and customer consent.

2

BSP server

Send a matching model

The home joins a group of similar homes and gets that group's client model.

3

Gateway

Train locally

The client model learns from this home's traffic. Raw data never leaves the house.

4

BSP server

Aggregate

Only parameters go up. FedAvg merges them into a better global model, round after round.

Initial gateway model

Client model per group

Global model at the provider

Source: FedHome, Section 4 and Figs. 3–4.

Walk left to right. The idea is hybrid FL: a generic gateway model, then a personalised model per group of similar homes, then federated averaging. Note that the grouping in step 2 is assumed in the experiments, not tested. We return to this in the critique.

Experimental setup

How the authors tested it

Datasets

UNSW HomeNet (4 testbeds, 105 devices) and an ARP-spoofing MITM dataset (4 sources)

Local models

Random Forest for devices, XGBoost for attacks: light enough for routers

FL framework

Flower with FedAvg; FedProx, FedNova and SCAFFOLD also compared

Clients

K = 2 labs in scenarios 1–4; K = 4 in scenario 5 and attack tests

Protocol

10 FL rounds × 5 independent runs, mean ± SD and 95% CI

Hardware

Raspberry Pi 4 (8 GB RAM, quad-core 1.5 GHz) as the gateway

Source: FedHome, Section 5.

Five device scenarios vary how similar the homes are: different brands, same brand but different model, identical devices, and identical device types spread over four testbeds. Keep the client count in mind: only two clients in most experiments.

Part 4 · Our critique

Can we trust the results?

Strengths first, then three problems: the method, the reported numbers, and the scale of testing.

Transition into our critique. Be clear we start with what the paper does well before the problems.

Our critique · First, what works

The paper's strengths

A real, well-motivated problem

Looks at security from the provider's side, which most IoT papers ignore, and proves the cross-dataset failure with data.

Designed for deployment

Chooses lightweight models over deep learning on purpose, and measures memory, time and bandwidth.

Repeated, reported runs

Five runs per scenario with standard deviations and confidence intervals; four aggregation methods compared.

Honest limitations

Admits few testbeds, a single attack type, and that no real router was used.

A good critique starts fair. The paper tackles a practical industry problem and thinks about real-world constraints. Now let us look at where the evidence is weaker.

Critique 1 · Method

The big gain may not come from federated learning

1. The comparison is unfair

The old method trained on one lab and was tested on the other, so it never saw those devices. FedHome trains on both labs. More diverse data, not necessarily federation, explains the jump. The fair test is FL vs. one model trained on all the data pooled.

Old method: trained on one lab

23–30%

FedHome: trained on both labs

83–93%

Pooled model, no FL (their Table 2)

99.9%

2. The method can't be reproduced

FedAvg (Eq. 1) averages a model's weights. Random Forest and XGBoost are sets of decision trees, so there are no weights to average.

The paper never says how the trees are merged, so nobody can repeat it.

w = Σ (nₖ / n) · wₖ ← for trees?

Source: FedHome, Eq. 1, Tables 2–3, Section 5.1.

Our most important point. The fair comparison is FL versus a centralized model trained on the pooled data, and versus each lab alone. Second, FedAvg is defined for parametric models like neural networks. Federated tree methods exist, such as federated XGBoost with histogram aggregation, but the paper does not say which one it used.

Critique 2 · Reported numbers

Several statistics don't add up

“1.000 ± 0.112”

Table 7: Scen. 1 rounds 8, 10; Scen. 2 rounds 2, 8, 10

A perfect 1.000 mean should have SD 0, not 0.112.

Mirrored SDs

Table 7, e.g. 0.482±0.372 and 1.000±0.372

Different means, identical SD (0.372): likely copied.

“Below 20%”

Section 5.1 text vs Table 3

Text says under 20%; Table 3 shows 23% and 30%.

No learning curve

Table 7, Scenarios 1 and 3

Round 1 is already near the best (0.940, 0.972): more rounds don't help.

Accuracy only

Tables 7–8

Only accuracy; baselines also report precision, recall, F1.

Source: FedHome, Tables 3, 7 and 8.

Anyone can check these directly in the tables. We are not accusing anyone; they may be typos or a script error. But they reduce confidence in the headline numbers, and a reviewer should ask the authors to explain them.

Critique 3 · Scale, deployment, privacy

Built for millions of homes, tested on two

2 clients

Claims scale for millions of homes but mostly tests 2 clients, and Scenario 5's homes are synthetic.

A Pi is not a router

It used 330 MB on an 8 GB Pi 4, but low-end home routers have only 64–128 MB.

Synthetic load test

CPU and memory were measured on generated data, not real home traffic.

Privacy assumed

Model updates can leak data, yet the paper adds no privacy protection or defence against poisoned updates.

ARP spoofing at home

It identifies devices using ARP spoofing, an attack technique, though the router already sees the traffic.

Untested pieces

Home grouping is assumed, not tested, and only one attack type (ARP MITM) is evaluated.

Source: FedHome, Sections 2.1, 4, 5.1, 5.3 and 5.4.

Also, the 15 GB versus 66 KB comparison is apples to oranges: a centralized system could send compact flow features instead of raw packets. And sharing model updates is not automatically private; research shows updates can leak training data.

Part 5 · Our new research

SecureFedHome

We turn every limitation we found into a research question, and design a fairer, safer, router-ready study.

Transition: a critique is only half the job. Now we propose our own follow-up study, SecureFedHome, that fixes the weaknesses we just showed.

From limitations to research

Each limitation becomes part of our study

Unfair baseline

Compare local-only, pooled centralized and FedHome on the same test sets

FedAvg on trees

Use a real federated tree method (e.g. federated XGBoost) or a small neural net, and document it

Only 2 clients

Simulate 50–100 homes with non-IID (Dirichlet) splits and clients dropping out

Accuracy only

Report macro-F1, per-class recall, false-alarm rate; fix and re-check Table 7

Pi, not router

Run on OpenWRT routers with 128–512 MB RAM using real traffic

Privacy & attacks

Add secure aggregation, test poisoning, extend to multi-attack data (CICIoT2023)

Our proposal, built on FedHome's own limitations and future work (Sections 5.4 and 6).

Each row answers one critique. The first row is the cheapest and most important: it tells us whether the gain comes from federated learning or simply from more data. If FedHome still matches pooled centralized training while keeping data private, the paper's claim becomes much stronger.

Our new study · Questions

What SecureFedHome will find out

Aim: find out whether federated learning really protects smart homes better, when tested fairly, privately and on real routers.

RQ1

Does FL still win against a fair baseline?

H1: FL comes within 3 points of pooled centralized macro-F1, and beats local-only training.

RQ2

Can it run on a real home router?

H2: a histogram-based federated XGBoost model needs under 128 MB of RAM.

RQ3

What do privacy and robustness cost?

H3: privacy noise and a poisoning defence cost under 5 points of macro-F1.

Three research questions, one per group of limitations. RQ1 fixes the unfair baseline. RQ2 fixes the Raspberry Pi problem. RQ3 adds the privacy and security testing the paper skipped. Each has a hypothesis we can prove or disprove with numbers.

Our new study · Design

How SecureFedHome works

At the home router (steps 1–3)

At the provider (steps 4–5)

1

Capture passively

Reads flow features from traffic it already forwards. No ARP spoofing.

2

Train locally

Histogram-based federated XGBoost: small enough for a router.

3

Protect the update

Adds privacy noise, then encrypts the update before sending.

4

Aggregate safely

Sees only the combined sum; discards updates that look poisoned.

5

Share the model

Sends the improved global model back to every home.

New: passive capture

Federated XGBoost

Differential privacy

Secure aggregation

Poisoning defence

Our proposal. Each step answers a limitation from Part 4.

Walk through the five steps. Steps one to three happen inside the home router, steps four and five at the provider. Point out what is new compared with FedHome: no ARP spoofing, a federated method that actually works for trees, privacy noise, encrypted aggregation, and a defence against hacked gateways sending poisoned updates.

Our new study · Experiments

A fair, realistic test plan

Data

CICIoT2023 (105 devices, 33 attacks) + UNSW HomeNet + our own 3-home lab capture

Homes

50 and 100 simulated homes, uneven (non-IID) data splits, 10% of homes dropping out each round

Baselines

Local-only · pooled centralized · FedHome (FedAvg) · ours, all on the same test sets

Hardware

3 OpenWRT routers (128, 256, 512 MB RAM) plus a Raspberry Pi 4 for comparison

Threats

10–30% hacked gateways sending poisoned updates (label flipping, scaled updates)

Metrics

Macro-F1, per-class recall, false-alarm rate, RAM, CPU time, bytes sent per round

Rigour

10 random seeds, mean ± SD, paired statistical tests; code and data released

Our proposal. CICIoT2023 is a public IoT attack dataset from the Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity.

This is how we answer the three questions. Many more homes than FedHome, uneven data like real life, every baseline on the same test sets, real routers, and attacks against the learning process itself. Ten repeated runs with proper statistical tests.
